I would say the only juror that can't be gender swapped without affecting the plot would be juror #3. The one that doesn't vote "Not guilty" until the very end.

The boy that is on trial is accused of killing his own father.

Juror #3 says he is also a father, but that his son no longer speaks to him, and this make him resent his kid. His reason to keep voting "Guilty" until the very end is him drawing parallels between the father and son of the case and his personal situation.

If he were a woman this comparison would not work (unless of course we also changed that the accused killed his mother).

The rest of jurors I think would work independently of their race or gender.

Is that commentary in the original film? The defendant's ethnicity is never mentioned in the original teleplay or the film's script, and he's clearly [White](https://youtu.be/lrE02PEqa6g?si=aunDmCl_omIf5_0E&t=156) in the movie. Juror 10, the bigoted garage owner, apparently holds all people not like him in disregard, focusing more on the youth's slum background than any specific characteristic.

Interestingly, I do agree with you that some level of commentary is lost with a diverse jury. I personally believe that it works best when all twelve jurors are of uniform identity characteristics. This is for two reasons. First, I think that if you start changing things up, you'll inevitably get people trying to read contemporary theories of race or gender relationships into it. Second, we're supposed to realize that there's a little bit of us in every single juror at that table. By making all the actors as similar as possible, this theme carries through more strongly.

Color-blind casting is only irrelevant in the wish fulfillment realm of the Shonda Rhimes streaming universe, and the same goes for gender bending casting. Realistically, it completely alters the context of the play, and it's a creative decision that could only fly on an amateur regional or high school production (for the sake of: everyone should get a role).
